passage: You think answering back is brave, Mahima? Listen to your Nani Madhuri. I was ten. My cousin broke Chachaji's clock, and Chachaji dragged me into the courtyard and scolded me in front of everyone. I knew I hadn't done it. My mouth opened and shut. In our house, answering an elder was worse than breaking ten clocks. So I stood there, eyes on my feet, and said nothing. For years after, I touched his feet at every festival, and every time something small and hot sat in my chest. When he was old he said once, 'You were always the quiet one.' I wish I had told him the truth that day, politely.

qa.q: What did the cousin break?
qa.a: Chachaji's clock.

qa.q: What did young Madhuri feel while standing silent in the courtyard?
qa.a: She felt afraid and ashamed, and also wronged, because she knew she hadn't done it but believed answering an elder was worse.

qa.q: At what moment in the story could a different choice have helped young Madhuri, and what might it have been?
qa.a: Later that same day, she could have told Chachaji calmly and politely that she had not broken the clock, or asked another adult to help her say it.

qa.q: How might Chachaji have seen young Madhuri's silence?
qa.a: Chachaji probably took it as respect or guilt, never knowing she was hurting, which is why years later he only called her 'the quiet one'.

grounding: Illustrates a child who stays silent under an unfair scolding because answering back is seen as disrespect, and whose swallowed hurt later turns into resentment.

passage:
The lights went out just as the guests' car turned into the lane. In the dark kitchen Dadaji tripped over a school bag and shouted, 'Hansa! How many times!'
It was Nitin's bag. Hansa's was hanging on its hook where it always was. Hansa, eleven, opened her mouth, then shut it. Mummy was lighting candles, Nitin was hiding behind the fridge, and the doorbell was ringing.
'Sorry, Dadaji,' she whispered, and moved the bag.
All evening she carried tea with a straight face and a polite smile. At night she lay stiff under the sheet, jaw tight, thinking, 'Next time I won't even say sorry. I won't say anything to him at all.'

qa.q: Whose bag did Dadaji trip over?
qa.a: Nitin's bag.

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling as she lay in bed that night?
qa.a: She felt angry and resentful about the unfair scolding, swallowing it so hard that she planned to stop speaking to Dadaji.

qa.q: How could Mummy or Dadaji help once the guests leave?
qa.a: Mummy could quietly ask Hansa what happened, and Dadaji could hear that it was Nitin's bag and say sorry, so the hurt does not harden into resentment.

qa.q: What might Nitin be feeling while hiding behind the fridge?
qa.a: Nitin is probably feeling guilty and scared, knowing it was Nitin's bag and that Hansa took the blame.

grounding: Shows a child who stays silent under an unfair scolding because talking back to an elder feels disrespectful, and whose swallowed feelings turn into resentment.

passage:
Monday: At tuition, Hafsa Aunty found a torn page in the library book and scolded Gautam in front of everyone. He hadn't torn it; the boy next to him had. Gautam looked at the floor and said nothing. You didn't answer back to Aunty.

Thursday: Gautam walked to tuition slowly, kicking a stone the whole way. When Aunty praised his sums, he didn't smile.

The next Monday: His little sister borrowed his eraser without asking, and Gautam shouted so loudly that Mummy came running. Later, on the stairs, he finally told her about the torn page. "I wanted to say it wasn't me. But you can't say that to Aunty."

Mummy sat beside him. "You can, politely. We'll go together tomorrow."

qa.q: Who actually tore the page?
qa.a: The boy next to him had torn it.

qa.q: Why did Gautam shout at his little sister?
qa.a: Gautam was carrying swallowed hurt and resentment from the unfair scolding, and it burst out over a small thing.

qa.q: What could help Gautam the next time an elder scolds him unfairly?
qa.a: Say calmly and politely that it wasn't him, or tell a parent that day so they can help, as Mummy offered.

qa.q: What would change if Hafsa Aunty knew the truth?
qa.a: Aunty might apologise or at least listen, and Gautam could enjoy her praise again instead of dreading tuition.

grounding: Shows a child who stays silent under an unfair scolding because answering back seems disrespectful, and whose swallowed hurt comes out later as resentment.

passage:
Yogesh, you've been sulking on my steps since your uncle shouted at you. Come, let old Hafsa Aunty tell you something.

When I was ten, in Bhopal, my Chacha found ink all over his accounts book. My cousin had spilled it, but Chacha shouted at me for five whole minutes. I stood with my hands behind my back and said nothing. Children didn't answer elders.

For years after, I wouldn't sit near him at Eid or laugh at his jokes. He never knew why.

When I was twenty, he asked me why I had always been cold to him. I told him about the ink. He was quiet a long time, then said, "Why didn't you tell me? I would have listened."

Maybe he would have. I lost ten years finding out.

qa.q: What had Hafsa's cousin spilled?
qa.a: Her cousin had spilled ink all over Chacha's accounts book.

qa.q: What did Hafsa feel toward her Chacha in the years after?
qa.a: She felt hurt and resentful, staying cold to him, not sitting near him at Eid or laughing at his jokes.

qa.q: What choice at ten might have changed the next ten years for Hafsa?
qa.a: Saying quietly and politely that her cousin had spilled the ink, or telling another adult that day, instead of swallowing it.

qa.q: How did Chacha feel when he finally learned about the ink?
qa.a: Chacha was quiet and seemed saddened, wishing Hafsa had told him because he would have listened.

grounding: Shows a child who stayed silent under an unfair scolding out of respect and fear, and whose swallowed feelings turned into years of resentment.

passage:
The school bus broke down in the pouring rain, and Kashish reached home an hour late, shoes squelching.

Dadu was waiting at the door. "Where have you been roaming? Do you know what time it is? No sense at all!"

Kashish opened her mouth to explain about the bus, then closed it. Dadu's face was red. You didn't argue with Dadu.

"Sorry, Dadu," she said, and went to change.

That evening, when Dadu set up the chessboard, she said she had homework. She said it the next evening too.

Her sister Ira, eight, climbed onto her bed. "Why don't you play chess with Dadu anymore?"

Kashish stared at the ceiling. "He didn't even ask why I was late."

"So tell him."

"You can't just tell Dadu things."

qa.q: Why was Kashish an hour late?
qa.a: The school bus broke down in the pouring rain.

qa.q: Why does Kashish keep saying she has homework when Dadu sets up the chessboard?
qa.a: Kashish feels hurt and resentful after the unfair scolding, and avoiding chess is how the swallowed feeling comes out.

qa.q: What small step could Kashish take with Dadu?
qa.a: Tell him calmly, perhaps over the chessboard, that the bus broke down and that it hurt to be scolded without being asked.

qa.q: What might it be like for Dadu when Kashish keeps skipping chess?
qa.a: Dadu may feel puzzled or hurt, not knowing his scolding was unfair or why she has gone quiet.

grounding: Shows a child who stays quiet under an unfair scolding because arguing feels disrespectful, and whose hurt later shows as quiet withdrawal.

passage:
The glass vase lay in pieces in the Nagpur drawing room. Tauji stood over Chetan, ten, his voice filling the flat. "Careless boy! Running inside like a goat!" Chetan had not run. His cousin Imran had knocked it with a cricket bat and gone upstairs. Chetan's throat burned. He looked at the floor and said nothing. Talking back to Tauji was not done, not ever. Mummy made him say sorry. He did, quietly.
That night, when his little sister took his pencil, Chetan shouted at her until she cried. He kicked his school bag across the room. Mummy came in. "What's wrong with you today?" He turned to the wall. Upstairs, he could hear Imran laughing at a cartoon. Chetan lay awake a long time, hot and hard inside, thinking about Tauji's finger pointing at him.

qa.q: Who actually knocked the vase?
qa.a: His cousin Imran, with a cricket bat.

qa.q: Why did Chetan shout at his little sister that night?
qa.a: He was holding in hurt and resentment from the unfair scolding, and it burst out at someone smaller.

qa.q: What could Mummy do to help Chetan now?
qa.a: She could sit with him calmly, ask what really happened with the vase, and let him tell it without calling it talking back.

qa.q: How might his little sister have experienced Chetan's shouting?
qa.a: She was probably frightened and confused, not knowing that his anger was really about Tauji.

grounding: It illustrates a child who stays silent under an unfair scolding because talking back is disrespectful, and whose swallowed feelings show later as resentment.
